title: Lisnagaver & Rasharkin
standfirst: Nineteenth-century records document several Glasgow households around Lisnagaver, Gortahar and Kilrea. Their shared older parentage, and any route back to Larne or Inishrush, remain open.

status.label: Confident Lisnagaver father links; upstream origins open

question: Which earlier family links are supported by the combined records, and how strong are they?
answer: John Glasgow, farmer, named in John-867’s 1846 marriage, is assessed 98% for that direct father relationship. Samuel’s father is confidently inferred at 95% from the explicit1851 brother relationship. Alexander’s father is confidently inferred at 90% from Nancy’s probate family network and the recorded Glasgow birth surnames. These strengthen the latter two earlier probable assessments without inventing a named parent statement. The 1796 Desertoghill identity and any Larne ancestry remain unproved; the Thomas–Daniel family is still separate. Jane Dysart’s inherited older-Alexander father is replaced locally by the same record-defined John, at 92% confident inference, from the explicit niece, baptism, will and family witness chain; Rosanna’s maternity remains separate.

chapters.title: Jane Dysart: a confident father replacement, 92%
body: Jane’s identity is anchored by Nancy Glasgow’s express niece Margaret Kennedy, the Rasharkin baptism naming Margaret’s mother Jane Glascaw, and James Dysart’s 1881 will naming daughter Margaret Kennedy, son Robert and granddaughter Mary Anne McCaughern. The 1892 probate citation coherently identifies Jane Dysart’s wider child group. Mary Anne’s appearance as a witness at Ann Glasgow’s 1875 marriage independently links the Dysart descendants to John Glasgow-867’s household. That John’s 1846 marriage names father John Glasgow, farmer. The combined kinship, recorded Glasgow birth surnames, compatible generations and matched households support the same record-defined father for Jane at 92% confident inference, replacing the unsupported older-Alexander pedigree.

No inspected record directly names Jane’s father. The citation is incomplete and is not an adjudicated pedigree; the underlying petition and heir schedule remain uninspected. John-867’s Ballydonnelly description and Lizzie remain unresolved. The witness association supports the family network but does not by itself prove kinship. A maternal half-sibling explanation involving different Glasgow fathers remains possible, without positive evidence favoring it. Alexander-3904 is chronologically compatible and retained as an unselected alternative, rather than declared impossible.

This subjective percentage assesses Jane’s father as the record-defined John Glasgow, farmer, named in John-867’s 1846 marriage. It does not identify the 1796 Desertoghill flax grower or establish John’s proposed Larne ancestry. Rosanna Unknown-761034 remains Jane’s separately unproved maternal attachment; this replacement does not identify John’s wife or prove a John–Rosanna marriage. Jane’s life dates and all existing relatives apart from the selected father are preserved. No live WikiTree edit is made.

chapters.title: Two confident inferences to John, farmer
body: Alexander’s independently documented children James, Mary and Ann match the 1892 citation’s Alexander-of-Rasharkin group. That group appears among heirs/next of kin before the separate legatee list. Nancy’s own niece/nephew statements, linked through the Dysart and Anderson baptisms, anchor the family interpretation. John-867’s distinctive James Garvin/Ann branch identifies the other cited household, and his 1846 marriage names father John Glasgow, farmer. Recorded Glasgow birth surnames favor a common paternal family. The combined identity and kinship argument supports a confident 90% inference; a generic unsupported half-sibling possibility does not impose a probable ceiling.

The 1851 Lisnagaver return explicitly calls Samuel the brother of John Glasgow-867. The head’s wife Margaret, 1846 marriage year, residence, parish and farming occupation uniquely fit John’s father-naming 1846 marriage. Samuel’s later unmarried weaver identity continues the same household man. On the ordinary meaning of the documented brotherhood and the shared Glasgow surname, John’s named father John Glasgow, farmer, is confidently Samuel’s father at 95%. No positive evidence supports a maternal-only half-brother relationship through another Glasgow father.

The probate citation is an incomplete service notice, not an adjudicated pedigree: Alexander’s living son Robert was omitted. John’s Ballydonnelly description and the cited Lizzie remain unexplained. The underlying petition and heir schedule have not been inspected. These are real limits, but no held competing household matches the James Garvin/Ann group and no evidence identifies different Glasgow fathers through a maternal half-sibling relationship. The flax-grower and older Larne identities remain separate hypotheses. The percentage concerns the selected father as John Glasgow, farmer, named in the 1846 marriage of John Glasgow-867. It does not identify him with the 1796 Desertoghill flax grower, establish his Larne ancestry, identify a mother or resolve Alexander’s separate death identity. Percentages are subjective evidence assessments, not calibrated statistical probabilities.

chapters.title: Glenleslie: John becomes a possible working father, 38%
body: The original 1851 Glenleslie household 21 return records John Glasgow as 100, Rose as 80, and 1791 for both. Its marriage heading asks “In what Year Married, or in what Years if more than once?” The detailed transcription’s first-marriage field is therefore an editorial description, not the literal question on this return. Only 1791 is entered: an earlier union is not documented, and the request for multiple years means its absence still weighs against a straightforward earlier-marriage explanation. The original also calls the forty-year-old John a nephew and gives his occupation as vagrant; the 1839 marriage belongs to him. The mortality table explicitly calls Andrew Glasgow, a thirty-year-old linen weaver who died of consumption in winter 1848, a son of the head. It does not name Andrew’s mother.

Select John Glasgow-1022 as the possible working father of the Glenleslie Robert represented by Glasgow-1367, at 38% subjective confidence. The original makes their reported age difference 28 years (100 versus 72), a comfortable father–son interval. They were Antrim-born Glasgow farmers in Glenleslie households 21 and 23, separated by the Hamill household. This is a specific nearby older family, and John is the best identified local father comparison already retained in the research. Reading the original marriage question removes the previous overstatement that it expressly records a first marriage in 1791. The combined generation and neighbouring-family argument is sufficient to select a weak working model rather than leave this preferred named comparison outside the tree; it is not a parent statement.

38% assesses the complete John-to-Robert profile hypothesis, not the certainty of reading the census. Robert’s census-implied birth about 1778–1779 precedes the sole reported marriage year by roughly twelve years. An earlier union, nonmarital fatherhood or a reporting error would still be needed, and none is established. The original asks for multiple marriage years, so omission of an earlier year remains a real limitation. John’s exceptional age may be inaccurate. An uncle, cousin, other collateral relative or unrepresented father remains possible; the older Alexander comparison is not excluded. Rose’s reported age does not fit her as Robert’s mother, and no mother or earlier wife is assigned. The selection concerns the 1851 Glenleslie man only: it does not identify him with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier, validate every attached child, or prove a Y-DNA pedigree. Hugh-3956’s 74% brother hypothesis includes a separate identity uncertainty and is not automatically assigned this father; his estimated earlier generation also needs its own chronology test. The [unnamed inherited father](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) is preserved as an uncertain alternative with no invented percentage. No live WikiTree family field is changed.

Earlier review: the22October unselected 18% assessment relied on the transcription’s express-first-marriage interpretation. That premise is superseded by the original column heading, while the sole1791 entry remains a genuine limitation. The saved prior assessment and its reasoning remain in both biographies and the structured relationship history.

Next useful test: Seek a tenancy succession, church entry, will or named-sibling record joining the Glenleslie household heads; compare an earlier John union and the collateral/older-Alexander explanations. The household-21 original has now been inspected and is no longer an outstanding access task.

chapters.title: John the watchmaker and Mary Black: Robert’s documented siblings
body: Research rationale: recover the named sibling family from the existing original-record chain before searching further generations. The named siblings provide firm family structure while their father remains uncertain.

John Glasgow, Prescott watchmaker with wife Jane in deed B13, is selected as Robert Glasgow-4150’s brother at 98% subjective confidence. Robert’s 1849 will gives brother John one sixth. John and Jane’s 1856 deed transfers an undivided one sixth of the same Dibble Street lots to Samuel, who is another will-named brother. The exact locality, buyer, parcels and fraction identify the grantor strongly; B13 does not itself expressly call John Robert’s brother. John’s birth, death and parents are not named, and his identity with an existing John profile is unresolved.

Mary Black, formerly Mary Glasgow, is Robert’s sister at 99% subjective confidence: C298 expressly states that relationship and traces her six children’s interests to Robert’s will, which names his sister Mary. Her children were John Black and Rose Ann Black of Drumoolish, Jane Miller and Agnes Black of Newburgh, Thomasina Montgomery of Legrand, Iowa, and Elizabeth Black, formerly of Newburgh. John’s wife Martha, Jane’s husband Robert Miller and Thomasina’s husband Mathew Montgomery also joined. Elizabeth, not Mary, is expressly deceased unmarried and intestate; her five siblings convey her share as heirs. Mary’s own birth, death, residence and husband’s forename remain unknown.

Extend the existing Alexander Glasgow-3904 father hypothesis to John and Mary at 27%, uncertain, conditional on their documented membership in the Prescott sibling family. Thomas-987 and Daniel-3896 already carry this father, and Samuel-4010 and Robert-4150 already have the same selected uncertain hypothesis. Its basis remains the single late descendant tradition naming Alexander as Thomas’s father, with compatible generation and sibling inference. The original will and deeds name no parent. These two extensions supply no independent parent testimony and do not raise the existing estimate; no mother is selected.

These are two previously unstructured record accounts recovered from evidence already researched in September, not two newly discovered sources or two proven additional distinct people. John retains six unselected compatible or weak existing-profile comparisons; later residence, spouse or death elsewhere is not by itself an exclusion of a possible migrant. No Mary Black/Glasgow match is established in the bounded local historical catalogue check. Both accounts remain on identity hold before any new WikiTree profile creation. Record dates are not birth dates.

Two strong sibling relationships enter the structured catalogue and family views: John–Robert 98% and Mary–Robert 99%. Two tentative father extensions to record accounts are 27%; no new confident father is established. The fixed and current historical-profile cohorts are unchanged: record-only identity accounts are not counted as newly distinct profiles or an improvement in paternal connectivity. Existing Robert–Alexander confidence and the earlier Larne reconstruction are unchanged.

Resolve John against the retained profile candidates using Jane, his watchmaking trade and the exact Prescott household. Compare the six Black children’s Irish and North American records for an identification of Mary and her husband. A contemporary source naming a parent remains the decisive question for Alexander; the later accounts cannot be counted twice.

chapters.title: Hugh and Robert at Glenleslie: probable brothers,74%
body: Research rationale: reconcile Mary’s explicit niece relationship and named father into the earliest defensible family degree; keep Glenleslie and Lisnagaver identities separate.

Select Hugh Glasgow-3956, the father named by Mary at her1862 marriage, as a probable brother of the1851 Glenleslie Robert represented within Glasgow-1367, at74% subjective confidence. Replace the existing uncertain father–son interpretation locally. The original1851 return expressly calls the unmarried34-year-old Antrim-born linen weaver Mary Glasgow Robert’s niece. The1862 Ballymena marriage expressly names the bride Mary Glasgow’s father as Hugh Glasgow,weaver. A same-surname niece whose father shares her weaving trade gives a coherent paternal-brother explanation; Hugh can belong to Robert’s generation without an invented intervening father. This promotes a long-recorded conditional inference into a selected working relationship, rather than discovering a new source or a new named relative.

The74% is a combined judgment about identity and relationship, not a calculated frequency. The census niece and1862 bride are probably, not certainly, the same Mary: the register gives full age and a residence apparently recorded as unknown, not a specific Glenleslie locator. The1851 age implies birth about1816/17; the1898 death age79 implies1818/19, a real one-to-three-year discrepancy. That death names Mary Montgomery,a labourer’s widow,and son John; it does not name her husband Thomas or give her maiden surname, so it is supporting context rather than independent proof of the full identity. Mary could instead be a different woman, and niece could express a maternal or marriage connection. No inspected record expressly calls Hugh Robert’s brother or names Hugh’s own parents.

This assessment concerns the Robert actually recorded at Glenleslie in1851. Glasgow-1367 also carries unresolved Lisnagaver and other identity comparisons; the brother inference neither identifies those property holders nor validates all children attached to that composite account. Hugh junior and Eliza’s1852/1854 Liminary marriages each name a Hugh Glasgow,weaver, but their father’s identity with Mary’s father remains a separate family reconstruction. Their shared residence supports their own sibling comparison; it does not independently prove Mary’s Glenleslie identity. No mother, new parent, shared anonymous parent, vital date, identity merge or live WikiTree field is added.

The previous captured father link from Hugh to Robert was explicitly uncertain and had no individual percentage. On this review, that father–son interpretation is retained as a less likely alternative explanation at17%, rather than treated as biologically disproved. Its earlier claim and original capture remain inspectable. It would require the census niece to be a different Mary, a non-paternal niece relationship, or a different family identification. The selected brother interpretation and the residual father interpretation are competing roles for the same two accounts, not two simultaneous links. These percentages do not exhaust all possible identities and relationships.

One existing relationship changes degree: uncertain father–son becomes probable brothers,74%. It adds zero new fathers and zero newly connected person pairs to the working family. Strict paternal connectivity must lose the old father edge; siblinghood is shown separately and is not counted as descent. Mary’s already confidently marked father Hugh is individually assessed99% for the express1862 record role; this is calibration of an existing confident relationship, not a new father or a certainty upgrade.

Seek a record carrying Mary or her father specifically between Glenleslie and the Montgomery marriage family, or a document naming Hugh and Robert as brothers. A birth, sibling marriage, tenancy succession or family notice could resolve the identity. Continue to assess the Liminary Hugh and Eliza family and Robert’s Lisnagaver identity separately.

chapters.title: Larne and Inishrush: James’s possible sons Adam, Alexander and John
body: Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father, at 27%, of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, at 17%, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other.

Reviewed 17 October 2026: extend the named James-1509 working father to [John Glasgow-822](/people/glasgow-822.html), very uncertain at 18%. John and Adam were nine years apart and headed the only two Glasgow households in the 1831 parish return; John's 1847 letter, intimate Inishrush/Tyanee family news and the James naming pattern support brotherhood or close collateral kinship. The father choice combines that unproved brotherhood with Adam's existing 27% James father hypothesis. These are correlated assumptions, not independent parent records; neither edge corroborates the other. No source names John as James's son or establishes a Larne-to-Inishrush migration. No mother is selected.

The older Adam-and-Maria parent model remains John's stronger unnamed rival, without invented placeholder parents. Adam-3902 himself was only about nine when John was born and cannot be John's father. Separately, John-822 is identified with [the Inishrush householder John-3927](/people/glasgow-3927.html) at 94%, from the Bible household, Inishrush and Drimbolg associations, 1847 letter and compatible emigration chronology. The census denomination is still disputed. That adult identity does not prove parentage, merge the accounts, change John-3927's captured placeholder father or strengthen the older Alexander reconstruction.

A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The two local 1740 Tamlaght Hugh households, including Glasgow-3931, and the older Adam-and-Maria naming model remain alternatives for Adam. A different unrecorded father remains possible. Neither Larne property succession nor the Inishrush household totals connect these generations. The 1831 return does not identify its unnamed occupants, and the later plot-29 succession is not evidence of James the ropemaker’s paternity. The shared [Glasgow-3905](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-3905) field is a recently created research placeholder, not evidence that Adam, older Alexander and Glasgow-1367 were brothers. It is not identified or merged with James. No father is extended to Glasgow-1367, and no unnamed extra generation is added.

Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. The 2007 account and its copied 2020 restatement are one source tradition, not independent witnesses. Daniel and Thomas are proved brothers, but their father’s name is not established by a contemporary parent record. The new James father therefore depends on that reconstructed older Alexander account. Younger Glasgow-951 remains a separate, unresolved possible brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel; the record-defined Glasgow-4090 remains his leading current father comparison. This batch does not select older Alexander as younger Alexander’s father or place that younger family beneath James. No Rosanna surname or October 1822 death date is newly established. James’s own Glasgow-1505 and Glasgow-1499 ancestry alternatives and existing children retain their earlier assessments.

The earlier Adam and older Alexander selections remain 27% and 17%, respectively. The 17 October review adds the conditional John-822 father at 18%, making three named father hypotheses, all uncertain. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics remain unchanged; mothers are independently unassigned. The earlier placeholder replacements remain limited to Adam and older Alexander, while John receives a new uncertain named-father selection. Captured WikiTree fields and rival parentage remain available. Counts describe retained profile accounts and conditional ancestry, not a proved pedigree.

chapters.title: A local network before the later families
body: The study keeps nearby Inishrush and Bann Valley material as comparison evidence, not as an inherited pedigree. Adam and John at Inishrush may be related, but no inspected record calls them brothers or names a shared parent.
The 1831 household return records separate Adam and John Glasgow households in Inishrush; it does not list household members by name.

chapters.title: Alexander and Mary’s documented family
body: Baptisms, the complete 1851 household and later marriages document Alexander Glasgow and Mary McCaughan and six children. Their descendant evidence places a tested line in R-FT20271.

John Glasgow, farmer, is Alexander’s probable father through Nancy’s reconstructed sibling group. Her newly inspected 1891 death notice gives about 75, conflicting with the age in her will; it confirms her Plattsburgh death and funeral but names no parents. The Glenleslie Nancy who died in 1847 is a different woman. Mary McCaughan’s parents remain unresolved.

PRONI reported no Glasgow or surname-variant mention under AG 57714 on 15 October 2026. The original enquiry prioritised Second Portglenone marriages, 1834–1838, but the result does not enumerate its actual record coverage. The separate Ballymoney Reformed Presbyterian family-register search, 1804–1844, is AG 57828 and remains outstanding. Neither the negative search nor the outstanding request changes the parentage assessment; the Lisnagaver rent-roll and map copy requests are also unresolved.

chapters.title: John and Margaret at Lisnagaver
body: The 1846 marriage, 1851 household and family memorial establish John Glasgow, Margaret Garvin, their children and John’s brother Samuel.

John’s original 1846 marriage names his father John Glasgow, farmer. The record-defined father is represented by Glasgow-4090; identifying him with the 1796 Desertoghill occupier or Glenleslie John is a separate unproved step.

chapters.title: Thomas and Daniel are brothers
body: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew. Daniel Neely’s marriage names Thomas as father.
That evidence proves the brotherhood and nephew relationship, but does not name Thomas and Daniel’s parents or prove Alexander was their brother.

Two Belfast death notices identify [Daniel Glasgow](/people/glasgow-3896.html) at Church Street, Kilrea, on 16 October 1871. They give age 73; his civil registration gives 75. These repeated notices corroborate the death date and address but leave a two-year birth-age discrepancy. They do not identify the brothers’ parents or connect them to Alexander’s family.

chapters.title: Later documented continuations
body: Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd’s marriage and original birth returns document daughters Sarah Taylor and Elizabeth Boyd. Mary Ann Glasgow’s marriage names Alexander as her father and later records continue the Elder household.

The original 6 January 1892 Belfast notice names [Jane Graham](/people/graham-21720.html) as wife of [Robert Glasgow](/people/glasgow-938.html). She died on 28 December at 534 Gallowgate, Glasgow, aged 51. The notice adds “formerly of Rasharkin” after Robert’s name. The exact death date and address strongly match Jane’s existing profile and support the couple’s Scottish continuation; the phrase is not assigned exclusively to Jane. It supplies no parents and does not identify the Robert in the separate 1861 neighbour report.
These continuations do not settle the older Glasgow-parentage question.

chapters.title: Lisnagaver newspaper context
body: The Belfast News-Letter of 5 June 1829 lists No. 2324, Alex. Glasgow, Lisnagaver, among applications to register freeholds under 10 Geo IV c. 8; the description gives lands in Kilconway barony and Lisnagaver townland. This is an application only: no age, kinship, admission or successful registration is stated.

The original page is now inspected, resolving the earlier access gap. [Alexander Glasgow-951](/people/glasgow-951.html) and [older Alexander Glasgow-3904](/people/glasgow-3904.html) remain compatible applicant candidates. The conflicting age estimates remain open; no parentage confidence changes.

A 7 January 1861 report names Robt. Glasgow as a Lisnagaver neighbour who warned James M’Caughern before a house collapse and narrowly escaped. [Robert Glasgow-938](/people/glasgow-938.html) and [Robert Glasgow-3449](/people/glasgow-3449.html) remain compatible candidates. No age, kinship or property bridge is stated.
